displayQuote: The only bad question is an unasked one

meta.title: Who really said "The only bad question is an unasked one"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Confucius — nothing like it is in the Analects, in Legge's English or in the Chinese. It is a twentieth-century classroom saying; the earliest dated form of 'no such thing as a stupid question' found so far is a Dear Abby column of 3 December 1970.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The only bad question is an unasked one'?
meta.ogDescription: No Chinese text exists for it. Confucius does praise asking questions — in the Analects he enters the grand temple and asks about everything — but this sentence is modern staffroom wisdom.

answer.label: Not Confucius — a modern classroom saying
answer.authorDates: Modern, anonymous · the family of sayings dated to 1970 and after
answer.sourceLine: It is not in the Analects, and there is no Chinese text for it — the decisive test, since the Analects is short, complete and fully concordanced in the original. What it belongs to is the modern ‘there is no such thing as a stupid question’ family, whose earliest dated instance anyone has produced is a Dear Abby column of 3 December 1970. Confucius does have a great deal to say about asking questions — it is one of his real preoccupations — but he never says this, and what he does say is sharper.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: 子入大廟，每事問。或曰：「孰謂鄹人之子知禮乎？入大廟，每事問。」子聞之曰：「是禮也。」
trail: We searched all twenty books of the Analects, in James Legge’s public-domain English and in the Chinese. No ‘bad question,’ no ‘stupid question,’ no unasked-question formula — and nothing in the Chinese that could produce one the searchable Analects ↗.

What is there is better. Book III, chapter 15: Confucius enters the grand temple and asks about everything, someone sneers that he evidently does not know the rites, and he replies that asking is the rite. That is a defence of question-asking made at his own expense, in public, under mockery Book III ↗.

And Book V, chapter 15 gives the phrase that Chinese speakers still use for this: 不恥下問 — Legge, ‘he was not ashamed to ask and learn of his inferiors.’ Confucius offers it as the reason a man was honoured with the title Wen. Shame, not stupidity, is the obstacle he names Book V ↗.

For the modern saying, the earliest dated instance we could find is a Dear Abby column in the Milwaukee Sentinel, 3 December 1970: ‘There is no such thing as a stupid question if it’s sincere.’ Carl Sagan later put a version of it in The Demon-Haunted World. Nobody has produced anything older, and we are not going to guess the modern trail ↗.
source.excerptNote: The genuine passage, in Chinese. Legge’s English: ‘The Master, when he entered the grand temple, asked about everything. Some one said, “Who say that the son of the man of Zou knows the rules of propriety! He has entered the grand temple and asks about everything.” The Master heard the remark, and said, “This is a rule of propriety.”’ He is being called ignorant for asking, and his answer is that asking is the correct behaviour.

source.rightsNote: Everything genuine here is free to reuse. The Chinese Analects is ancient, and James Legge’s English (1861–1893) is long out of copyright, so both the temple passage and the ‘not ashamed to ask’ line can be quoted without permission — which is a good reason to quote those instead of the modern slogan. Modern translations of the Analects (Waley, Lau, Slingerland, Watson and others) are all in copyright and produce different wordings. The 1970 newspaper column and Carl Sagan’s book are likewise protected. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Confucius
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Confucius
author.metaLine: 551–479 BC · Chinese teacher and philosopher (here, the misattributed figure)
author.bio: Confucius (Kong Qiu, 551–479 BC) was, above everything else, a teacher, and the Analects is largely a record of him being asked things and answering. Questions are the book’s literal form. That makes him a magnetic false author for any classroom slogan — and it also makes the fakes unnecessary, because the real material on the subject is better: a man who asked about every object in a temple while onlookers laughed, and who thought the only thing standing between you and knowing was your embarrassment.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This one has been asked publicly for years without a straight answer — a literature forum thread on it has passed eleven thousand views with nothing accepted. Here is what the sources actually support.

items.why: Twenty books, roughly five hundred passages, searchable in the original: nothing corresponds. And no proposed Chinese wording circulates alongside the English, which is the pattern for a modern invention rather than a translation check the text ↗.

The one unaccepted answer on Stack Exchange offers ‘the man who asks a question is a fool for a minute, the man who does not ask is a fool for life’ as the Confucian original. That is a separate proverb, usually labelled Chinese or Japanese, and itself unverified. Neither is in the Analects.

Variants circulate under both names on Goodreads and Quora with nothing attached — no book, no interview, no date. Einstein in particular functions as a general-purpose signature for any sentence about curiosity.

‘There is no such thing as a stupid question if it’s sincere’ — Dear Abby, 3 December 1970. That is the oldest dated instance anyone has produced for the family. It may well be older; nobody has shown it the dated citation ↗.

Analects III.15, the grand temple; V.15, ‘not ashamed to ask and learn of his inferiors’; and XV.16, where the Master says of a man who never asks ‘what shall I think of this?’ that he can do nothing with him. All in Legge, all public domain, all quotable with a chapter number.

misattribution.truthLine: Not Confucius — no Chinese exists for it and nothing like it is in the Analects. It belongs to the modern ‘no stupid questions’ family, dated no earlier than 1970 the modern trail ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: Every teacher, manager and induction session needs a sentence that gives people permission to admit they are lost, and this one does the job in eight words. The Confucius signature is a bolt-on: it converts a kindness into a rule, which is more persuasive to the person too embarrassed to raise a hand.

What is a shame is that the real thing is more useful. Confucius does not tell you your question is fine; he tells you a story about being publicly mocked for asking too many, and shrugs that asking was the correct behaviour. That is a better argument, because it concedes that you will look foolish and says do it anyway.
context.detailsSummary: What Confucius actually says about asking
detailsBody: Analects III.15 — entering the grand temple, he asks about everything; told this proves he does not know the rites, he answers that this is the rite. Legge’s English is public domain.
Analects X.14 repeats the temple detail in the chapter describing his daily conduct: on entering the ancestral temple of the state, he asked about everything.
Analects V.15 — Kong Wenzi earned his honorific because he was ‘of an active nature and yet fond of learning, and he was not ashamed to ask and learn of his inferiors’: 不恥下問.
Analects XV.16 — the reverse case: ‘When a man is not in the habit of saying, “What shall I think of this? What shall I think of this?” I can indeed do nothing with him!’
Analects XIX.6, from his student Zi Xia rather than the Master: learning extensively, inquiring with earnestness, reflecting with self-application.
Every one of these can be cited with a book and chapter number. That is what a real quotation looks like.
context.pull: He does not say your question is fine. He says he was mocked for asking, and that asking was correct.
